title: A Clearer Picture of AI and the College Job Market
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill revisits the contested question of whether generative AI is eroding early-career job prospects for college graduates, a question he admits he had mostly dodged because the data were not compelling. The occasion is a new Census Bureau working paper that links bachelor's graduates' majors to actual employment and earnings records, grouping 142 majors into deciles by their estimated exposure to AI. Hill walks through the paper's figures, which he has rebuilt as interactive charts, showing that graduates from the most AI-exposed fields became less likely to find work right after graduation, earned substantially less, and shifted into lower-paying sectors after ChatGPT arrived. He is careful about the study's limits: exposure is inferred rather than observed, the sample leans on public research universities, and above all the analysis cannot separate AI's effect from the pandemic-era tech hiring correction that was already underway. Setting the paper beside Burning Glass and Stanford payroll research, he concludes that AI is increasingly likely to be adding to an already difficult transition from college to work, even though the size of that effect remains unresolved.
points: A Census Bureau working paper that follows graduates into whatever jobs they actually land, including the 'unintentional barista' outcome, gives the strongest evidence yet on AI-exposed majors.

After ChatGPT-3.5, graduates of the most AI-exposed majors were less likely to be employed right after graduation and saw substantial earnings declines, with employment shifting toward retail and food service.

The study's central weakness is that computer science and related majors were hit simultaneously by AI and by the reversal of the pandemic tech hiring boom, so the two causes cannot be cleanly separated.

Hill's verdict is a measured one: AI probably added to deterioration already visible in 2022, but how much of the damage it caused remains an open question for institutions rethinking program outputs.
quotes: I have mostly chosen the Brave Sir Robin approach, saying that it’s too early to tell while running away. More seriously, the data have not been compelling enough to know.
Taken together, the emerging research makes it increasingly likely, in my judgment, that AI is adding to the deterioration in early-career opportunities.
This treatment includes the unintentional barista problem of our economy, and too many studies looking primarily at occupations miss this problem.

Overall, our results suggest that there was a fairly immediate and concentrated deterioration in the early labor market outcomes of graduates from the most AI-exposed fields following the introduction of ChatGPT-3.5.

Employment shifted away from relatively high-paying sectors such as Information and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services and toward lower-paying sectors such as Retail Trade and Accommodation and Food Services.
The fields most exposed to AI—particularly computer science and related majors—were also heavily exposed to the reversal of the pandemic-era tech hiring boom.
That correction was underway before ChatGPT launched in November 2022. The central question is therefore how much graduates’ prospects would have deteriorated even without generative AI.

In my view, the accumulating evidence makes it increasingly likely that AI added to the deterioration already in place in 2022, especially for recent graduates, while the size of separate effects remains unresolved.
